newsitem.title: CYPRUS: IMF backs Cyprus policies, but some reforms needed.
newsitem.headline: IMF backs Cyprus policies, but some reforms needed.

text.p: IMF officials visiting Cyprus have given the economy a clean bill of health, but the island needs to change its law on interest rates and amend its cost-of-living wage settlements, the IMF mission leader said on Thursday.

The eastern Mediterranean island should eliminate interest rate ceilings and reform its wage-settlement methods to reduce its vulnerability to external shocks, Maria Carcovic told Reuters in an interview.
"On international standards it is an economy which has done remarkably well," she said.
"In a big part this is due to the prudence in fiscal and monetary policies for a number of years, such that they have lent credibility to the peg (of the Cyprus pound) to the ECU."
An IMF team will return to the island next year for a full consultation on the economy, she said.

Cyprus enjoys low inflation and unemployment and expects nominal GDP growth of 2.5 percent this year compared with 5.0 percent in 1995. The decline in the expected growth rate is largely attributable to tourism, which comprises 21 percent of GDP.
Official figures have not been released, but the number of tourist arrivals in the first eight months of 1996 fell five percent compared with the same period last year.
Carcovic, heading a staff mission to Cyprus, said the IMF was concerned at a rigidity in the financial and labour markets.

"First and foremost we would like to see an elimination of the interest rates law, and the elimination of COLA," she said, referring to a cost of living allowance added to wages twice a year, based on increases in the consumer price index.

The government has expressed its commitment to abolishing the interest rate ceiling of nine percent in force for more than 50 years. It has set a target date of end-1997 or the beginning of 1998, when entry negotiations with the European Union are due to start.
Discussions on modifying the COLA system are currently in progress between unions and employers, but the unions are refusing to accept any change.
One of the disadvantages of a rigid system of wage determination is reduced labour mobility, hampering movement from declining to emerging sectors of the economy, Carcovic said,
